modernNote: Modern comparisons are our own, based on public reporting. These people aren't connected to Zelos and don't endorse it.
note: Hall of Minds (owner 2026-10-22). Historical figures only; portraits are public-domain paintings. Quotes are checked against the source given; 'plain' and 'trading' are our own explanations. Edit here; scripts/build_practice.py copies it to functions/minds.json.

figures.name: Aristotle
figures.tagline: The teacher of Alexander the Great, who wrote down how good habits are built.

lessons.title: You become what you practice
text: Aristotle taught that nobody is born brave, fair or skilled. You become brave by doing brave things, again and again, until it is who you are.
Skill is not a gift you wait for. It is the sum of what you repeat.
lessons.trading: Good trading is a habit, not a mood. Follow the same checklist on every trade, even the boring ones, until you do it without thinking.

lessons.title: The golden middle
text: Aristotle said most good qualities sit between two bad ones. Courage sits between being reckless and being a coward.
Too much of a good thing turns into a bad thing.
lessons.trading: Risk works the same way. Risking nothing teaches you nothing; risking too much wipes you out. The middle is a small, fixed amount on every trade.

lessons.title: One good day is not a season
text: He said one swallow does not make a spring. A single good day does not make a happy life.
What counts is the long run.
lessons.trading: One big win doesn't prove your method works, and one loss doesn't prove it fails. Judge yourself on 20 or more trades, not one.

lessons.title: Feel it, but aim it
text: Aristotle didn't say never get angry. He said anyone can get angry; doing it at the right time, for the right reason, by the right amount, is the hard part.
Emotions are fine. Being run by them isn't.
lessons.trading: After a loss you will want to win it back fast. That is revenge trading. Notice the feeling, close the app, and come back to your plan tomorrow.

quotes.text: For as it is not one swallow or a fine day that makes a spring, so it is not one day or a short time that makes a man blessed and happy.
quotes.source: Nicomachean Ethics, Book I, ch. 7 (W. D. Ross translation)
quotes.plain: One good day doesn't make a good life. Only a long run of them does.
quotes.trading: Don't judge a strategy on one trade. Judge it on many.

quotes.text: For the things we have to learn before we can do them, we learn by doing them, e.g. men become builders by building and lyre-players by playing the lyre.
quotes.source: Nicomachean Ethics, Book II, ch. 1 (W. D. Ross translation)
quotes.plain: You learn a skill by doing it, not just by reading about it.
quotes.trading: Practice trades teach you more than any video. That's why Zelos gives you practice money.

quotes.text: It is a mean between two vices, that which depends on excess and that which depends on defect.
quotes.source: Nicomachean Ethics, Book II, ch. 6 (W. D. Ross translation)
quotes.plain: The right way is usually in the middle, between too much and too little.
quotes.trading: Not too big, not too small: risk the same modest amount on every trade.

quotes.text: Any one can get angry—that is easy—or give or spend money; but to do this to the right person, to the right extent, at the right time, with the right motive, and in the right way, that is not for every one, nor is it easy.
quotes.source: Nicomachean Ethics, Book II, ch. 9 (W. D. Ross translation)
quotes.plain: Having feelings is easy. Using them well, at the right time and amount, is hard.
quotes.trading: A loss will make you want to act. Wait until you are calm, then act on your plan.

story: Aristotle was born in 384 BC in Stagira, in northern Greece. His father was the doctor to the king of Macedon.
At 17 he went to Athens to study at Plato's Academy, the best school in the Greek world, and stayed for about 20 years.
After Plato died, he travelled. On the island of Lesbos he studied sea creatures up close, one of the first people to do science by careful watching.
In 343 BC King Philip asked him to teach his son, the future Alexander the Great.
Back in Athens he opened his own school, the Lyceum. He wrote about almost everything: logic, animals, the stars, politics, poetry and how to live a good life.
He left Athens in 323 BC, when feeling turned against anyone linked to Macedon, and died the next year.

carried.title: He looked for himself
carried.text: Aristotle described hundreds of animals from careful watching and dissection, and noticed things others missed, such as dolphins breathing air and feeding their young with milk.
carried.source: Aristotle, History of Animals

carried.title: Collect the evidence
carried.text: To understand which governments work, his school collected and studied the constitutions of 158 Greek cities instead of just theorizing.
carried.source: Aristotle, Constitution of the Athenians (the one that survives)

carried.title: Teaching on the move
carried.text: He taught while walking up and down the covered walkways of the Lyceum, so his followers became known as the 'Peripatetics', the walkers.
carried.source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of the Eminent Philosophers, Book 5

carried.title: Truth over his teacher
carried.text: He disagreed openly with his own teacher Plato, writing that, though friends and truth are both dear, it is right to honor truth first.
carried.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics, Book I, ch. 6

text: Charlie Munger, Warren Buffett's late business partner, told people to build a 'latticework of mental models': the big ideas from many subjects, not just one.
That's very close to how Aristotle worked: he studied animals, politics, logic and ethics, and used each to understand the others.
thenNow.trading: Don't learn only charts. Learn a little about how businesses, the economy and people's emotions work; each makes you read the chart better.

figures.name: Alexander the Great
figures.tagline: Taught by Aristotle, he built one of the largest empires in history before he was 30.

lessons.title: Learn from the best before you lead
text: As a teenager, Alexander was taught by Aristotle himself. He kept a copy of Homer's Iliad with him on campaign.
He studied the great before trying to become one.
lessons.trading: Before you trade a setup with practice money, study it. Read how it works, look at old charts, then try it.

lessons.title: Move before the other side is ready
text: Alexander often moved faster than his enemies thought possible, and struck before they were set.
Speed won battles that numbers alone would have lost.
lessons.trading: In trading, speed means having your plan ready before the market opens: your entry, your stop, your target. Then you act, instead of deciding in a rush.

lessons.title: Cut the knot
text: Legend said whoever untied the Gordian Knot would rule Asia. Alexander didn't untie it. He cut it with his sword.
Sometimes the answer is to stop fiddling and solve the problem directly.
lessons.trading: If a trade hits your stop, don't search for reasons to stay in. The stop is the sword: cut it and move on.

lessons.title: Lead from the front
text: Alexander rode into battle at the front of his cavalry and was wounded many times. His soldiers followed because he took the same risks.
People trust leaders who share the danger.
lessons.trading: If you post a trade idea in your squad, take it yourself in your practice account. Own your calls, wins and losses.

quotes.text: I will not steal a victory.
quotes.source: Plutarch, Life of Alexander, ch. 31 (before the battle of Gaugamela, when told to attack at night)
quotes.plain: He wanted to win fair and in the open, so nobody could say it was luck or a trick.
quotes.trading: A win you don't understand teaches you nothing. Win by your rules, so you can do it again.

quotes.text: If I were not Alexander, I would be Diogenes.
quotes.source: Plutarch, Life of Alexander, ch. 14
quotes.plain: He admired the poor philosopher Diogenes, who wanted nothing, as much as he loved his own power.
quotes.trading: Wanting less is a strength. A trader who doesn't need every trade can wait for the good ones.

quotes.text: Is it not worthy of tears that, when the number of worlds is infinite, we have not yet become lords of a single one?
quotes.source: Plutarch, Moralia, On Tranquillity of Mind, ch. 4
quotes.plain: Even when he had a lot, he felt he had too little. His hunger never ended.
quotes.trading: Ambition drives you, but greed sinks accounts. Set a goal, and know when to stop for the day.

story: Alexander was born in 356 BC in Macedon, in northern Greece, the son of King Philip II, who had built the strongest army of the time.
From 13 to 16 he was taught by the philosopher Aristotle. He loved Homer's Iliad and dreamed of being a hero like Achilles.
His father was murdered in 336 BC, and Alexander became king at 20. Two years later he crossed into Asia to take on the huge Persian Empire.
He beat the Persians at the Granicus river, at Issus and finally at Gaugamela in 331 BC, took Egypt (where he founded the city of Alexandria), and pushed on as far as India.
In India his exhausted army refused to go further, and he had to turn back. He died in Babylon in 323 BC, aged 32, and his generals split his empire between them.

carried.title: Watching before acting
carried.text: As a boy, Alexander tamed the wild horse Bucephalus, which no one could ride. He'd noticed the horse was scared of its own shadow, so he turned it to face the sun.
carried.source: Plutarch, Life of Alexander, ch. 6

carried.title: Sharing the thirst
carried.text: Crossing a desert where his army was dying of thirst, soldiers brought him a helmet of water. He poured it on the ground, because his men had none.
carried.source: Arrian, The Campaigns of Alexander, Book 6, ch. 26

carried.title: First over the wall
carried.text: Attacking a town in India, he climbed the ladder first and jumped inside the walls almost alone. An arrow went through his chest, and he nearly died.
carried.source: Arrian, The Campaigns of Alexander, Book 6, ch. 9–11

carried.title: Scars as proof
carried.text: When his army mutinied, he reminded them that he had shared every danger, saying there was no part of his body, except his back, without a scar.
carried.source: Arrian, The Campaigns of Alexander, Book 7, ch. 10

figures.name: Napoleon Bonaparte
figures.tagline: A young officer who rose to rule France and rewrote how wars are fought.

lessons.title: Study the greats
text: Napoleon read the campaigns of Alexander, Hannibal and Caesar over and over. He told officers to model themselves on them.
He didn't start from zero. He started from the best.
lessons.trading: You don't have to invent a strategy. Learn a proven one first (Trading 101, the Strategy library), then make it your own.

lessons.title: Speed is a weapon
text: His armies marched faster than anyone in Europe, living off the land instead of waiting for supply wagons.
He said the strength of an army is its mass times its speed.
lessons.trading: Being prepared is what lets you act fast. Have your watchlist and levels ready, so when price reaches your level you place the order, not start thinking.

lessons.title: Bring everything to one point
text: Napoleon's favorite move was to gather his forces at one place and hit the enemy's weakest point with all of it.
Spread thin, you are weak everywhere.
lessons.trading: Ten tiny trades at once means you watch none of them. Focus on the 1 to 3 best setups you understand.

lessons.title: The mind wins three quarters
text: Napoleon believed morale counted three times more than numbers or guns. Tired, scared troops lose.
How people feel decides how they fight.
lessons.trading: Your mood is part of your strategy. Tired, angry or bored? Don't trade. Take a break and keep your edge for when you're sharp.

quotes.text: Read over and over again the campaigns of Alexander, Hannibal, Caesar, Gustavus, Turenne, Eugene, and Frederic. Model yourself upon them.
quotes.source: The Military Maxims of Napoleon, Maxim 78 (collected 1827; English edition 1831)
quotes.plain: Study the best people in your field again and again, and copy how they did it.
quotes.trading: Replay great trades, yours and others'. Ask: why did this work, and could I see it coming?

quotes.text: The strength of an army, like the quantity of motion in mechanics, is estimated by the mass multiplied by the velocity.
quotes.source: The Military Maxims of Napoleon, Maxim 9 (English edition 1831)
quotes.plain: Being big isn't enough; you also have to be quick.
quotes.trading: A good idea entered too late is a bad trade. Plan early so you can act on time.

quotes.text: In war, three-quarters turns on personal character and relations; the balance of manpower and materials counts only for the remaining quarter.
quotes.source: Napoleon, note on the affairs of Spain, 27 August 1808 (Correspondance de Napoléon Ier)
quotes.plain: Mindset matters more than tools. Three parts mind, one part everything else.
quotes.trading: Discipline beats a fancy indicator. Most losses come from breaking your own rules.

story: Napoleon was born in 1769 on Corsica, an island France had taken over the year before. At nine he was sent to a military school in France, where other boys mocked his accent and his family's lack of money. He spent his free time reading history.

He became an artillery officer. In 1793, aged 24, he worked out how to drive the British fleet out of the port of Toulon: take the hills above the harbor and put cannons there. It worked, and he was made a general.
In 1796 he was given France's army in Italy: hungry, unpaid and losing. Within months he won battle after battle, mostly by moving faster than his enemies and hitting them one at a time.
In 1799 he seized power, and in 1804 he crowned himself Emperor. He also rewrote France's laws into one clear code, the Napoleonic Code, which is still the base of the law in many countries.
His greatest win was Austerlitz in 1805. Then he overreached: a long war in Spain, and in 1812 an invasion of Russia that cost him most of his army.
He was exiled in 1814, escaped and came back for 100 days, and lost for good at Waterloo in 1815. He died in exile on the island of Saint Helena in 1821.

carried.title: Fighting next to his men
carried.text: At Lodi in 1796, Napoleon was seen at the front aiming the cannons himself, a job for an ordinary corporal. His soldiers started calling him "the little corporal", a nickname that stuck for life.
carried.source: As told in Andrew Roberts, Napoleon: A Life (2014)

carried.title: Leading from the bridge
carried.text: At Arcole the same year, with his attack stalled, he grabbed a flag and led a charge onto the bridge himself, and ended up knocked into a marsh.
carried.source: As told in David Chandler, The Campaigns of Napoleon (1966)

carried.title: He knew his soldiers
carried.text: He was famous for remembering veterans' names and battles, stopping to talk to them and teasingly pulling their ears, which made ordinary soldiers feel seen by the Emperor.
carried.source: From the memoirs of his valet Constant and Las Cases' Memorial of Saint Helena

carried.title: He studied everything
carried.text: His secretary described him working through reports, numbers and maps late into the night, asking officers, engineers and locals about roads, rivers and supplies until he knew the ground better than they did.
carried.source: Baron Fain, Memoirs (published 1908)

text: Like Napoleon, Elon Musk is known for very long working weeks, getting into the smallest details himself, and deadlines that most people think are impossible.
Both used speed as a weapon: Napoleon out-marched his enemies, and SpaceX tests rockets, learns from the ones that blow up, and rebuilds faster than older companies.
Both stories also show the risk: taking on too much at once.
thenNow.trading: Speed and hands-on work win, but only with a limit you respect. Plan fast, act fast, and stop for the day when you hit your loss limit.

figures.name: Julius Caesar
figures.tagline: A general and writer who turned the Roman Republic into an empire.

lessons.title: Cross the Rubicon
text: In 49 BC, Caesar led his army across the Rubicon river into Italy. By law that meant civil war. There was no going back.
Once he decided, he committed fully.
lessons.trading: Decide your plan before the trade, then follow it. Changing your stop in the middle of a trade is how small losses become big ones.

lessons.title: People believe what they want to
text: Caesar wrote that people usually believe what they wish were true. He used it against his enemies, and guarded against it in himself.
Wanting something to be true doesn't make it true.
lessons.trading: Once you're in a trade, you'll look for news that agrees with you. Ask instead: what would prove me wrong? Then watch for that.

lessons.title: Small causes, big changes
text: Caesar noticed that in war, tiny events (a rumor, a wrong turn, a sudden storm) often decided great battles.
Small things are not always small.
lessons.trading: One surprise headline can move a stock 10% overnight. That's why you size every trade so a surprise can't hurt you badly.

lessons.title: Write it down
text: Caesar wrote his own account of his wars, the Commentaries, in short, clear sentences. He controlled the story and remembered the lessons.
What gets written down gets learned.
lessons.trading: Keep a trading journal: why you entered, how it ended and what you felt. Your notes become your best teacher.

quotes.text: Veni, vidi, vici. (I came, I saw, I conquered.)
quotes.source: Caesar's report of his quick victory at Zela, 47 BC (Suetonius, Life of Julius Caesar, 37; Plutarch, Life of Caesar, 50)
quotes.plain: It was so quick and clear that three words were enough.
quotes.trading: The best trades are usually simple. If you need a long story to justify one, skip it.

quotes.text: The die is cast. (Alea iacta est.)
quotes.source: Suetonius, Life of Julius Caesar, 32 (crossing the Rubicon, 49 BC)
quotes.plain: The decision is made, and we live with it.
quotes.trading: Once your order is in, let your plan run. Don't keep second-guessing it.

quotes.text: Men willingly believe what they wish.
quotes.source: Caesar, Commentaries on the Gallic War, Book III, ch. 18
quotes.plain: People believe things because they want them to be true.
quotes.trading: Hoping a stock goes up is not a reason to hold it. Your stop is your reality check.

quotes.text: Fortune, which has great power in all matters and especially in war, brings about great changes by small causes.
quotes.source: Caesar, Commentaries on the Civil War, Book III, ch. 68
quotes.plain: Small, random things can change everything, so be ready for surprises.
quotes.trading: Never risk so much that one surprise can knock you out.

story: Julius Caesar was born in 100 BC into an old Roman family that had more name than money.
As a young man he was captured by pirates. He joked with them, wrote poems while he waited for the ransom, and told them he'd come back and punish them. He did.
He climbed Rome's political ladder by spending huge sums on games and favors, borrowing heavily, and making a deal with Rome's two most powerful men, Pompey and Crassus.
From 58 to 50 BC he conquered Gaul (roughly today's France and Belgium) and wrote short, clear reports on the war that are still read today.

In 49 BC he crossed the Rubicon river with his army, starting a civil war, and won it. He made himself dictator, and among many reforms he fixed the calendar: our 365-day year with a leap day comes from him.
Many senators feared he would make himself king, and on the Ides of March (15 March) 44 BC a group of them stabbed him to death.

carried.title: Calm under pressure
carried.text: Held by pirates, Caesar told them their ransom was too low and to ask for more. He treated them like his guards, and promised to come back and punish them. Once free, he raised ships and did.
carried.source: Plutarch, Life of Caesar, ch. 2

carried.title: Into the front line
carried.text: At the river Sabis in 57 BC, with his army about to break, Caesar grabbed a shield from a soldier, pushed to the front and called his officers by name until the line held.
carried.source: Caesar, Commentaries on the Gallic War, Book II, ch. 25

carried.title: "Comrades"
carried.text: He called his troops "comrades" rather than "soldiers", and they followed him through ten years of war.
carried.source: Suetonius, Life of Julius Caesar, ch. 67

carried.title: Mercy as a strategy
carried.text: After winning the civil war, he pardoned many of his enemies instead of killing them, a choice that won him support (and, in the end, let some of his killers live).
carried.source: Suetonius, Life of Julius Caesar, ch. 75

figures.name: Benjamin Franklin
figures.tagline: Printer, inventor, scientist and statesman, who became rich by being careful and steady.

lessons.title: Money makes money
text: Franklin explained to young businessmen how money grows: money earns more money, and that money earns more too.
He left money in his will to Boston and Philadelphia to grow for 200 years. It did.
lessons.trading: Small, steady gains add up. 1% a month, kept and grown, beats a lucky double that you give back.

lessons.title: Time is money
text: Franklin said an hour wasted is money lost, because you could have earned in that time.
He planned every hour of his day on a written schedule.
lessons.trading: Set your trading time and your learning time. Watching charts all day isn't working; it usually leads to bad trades.

lessons.title: Track yourself
text: Franklin picked 13 habits to build and kept a little chart, marking each day he slipped.
He couldn't fix what he didn't measure.
lessons.trading: Score yourself after each trading day: did I follow my plan? Your Zelos history and win rate show the numbers. Your journal shows why.

lessons.title: Haste makes waste
text: Franklin printed sayings like this in Poor Richard's Almanack, a yearly book of plain advice.
Rushing costs more than it saves.
lessons.trading: Chasing a stock that already ran usually means buying the top. If you missed it, wait for the next setup.

quotes.text: Remember that time is money.
quotes.source: Advice to a Young Tradesman, 1748
quotes.plain: Time you waste is money you could have made.
quotes.trading: Spend your trading time on planning and review, not on staring at the screen.

quotes.text: Money can beget money, and its offspring can beget more, and so on.
quotes.source: Advice to a Young Tradesman, 1748
quotes.plain: Money you keep and invest earns more money, and then that earns more too.
quotes.trading: Protect your account first. A big loss stops your money from growing.

quotes.text: Lost time is never found again.
quotes.source: Poor Richard's Almanack, 1748
quotes.plain: You can't get back time you wasted.
quotes.trading: Learn from every loss right away, so the time it cost you isn't wasted.

quotes.text: Well done is better than well said.
quotes.source: Poor Richard's Almanack, 1737
quotes.plain: Doing something matters more than talking about it.
quotes.trading: Talking about trades is easy. Follow your plan in your account; that's what counts.

story: Benjamin Franklin was born in Boston in 1706, the 15th of 17 children. His family could only afford two years of school.
At 12 he started work in his brother's print shop. At 17 he ran away to Philadelphia with almost no money and no friends there.
He built his own printing business with long hours and a reputation for being reliable. His yearly book of advice, Poor Richard's Almanack, made him famous.

At 42 he had enough money to step back from business, and spent his time on science and his city: he proved lightning is electricity, invented the lightning rod and bifocal glasses, and started a library, a fire company and a university.
He then became a diplomat. In Paris he won France to America's side in its war for independence, and he signed both the Declaration of Independence and the US Constitution.
He died in 1790, one of the most famous people in the world.

carried.title: He taught himself to write
carried.text: Without schooling, he took essays he admired, wrote them out again from memory, then compared his version with the original to find his mistakes.
carried.source: Franklin, Autobiography

carried.title: He let people see the work
carried.text: As a young printer he made a point of being seen working, and sometimes pushed his own paper home through the streets in a wheelbarrow, so people knew he was hardworking and could be trusted.
carried.source: Franklin, Autobiography

carried.title: A club for getting better
carried.text: At 21 he started the Junto, a weekly club of young tradesmen who met to swap ideas, books and advice on improving themselves and their city.
carried.source: Franklin, Autobiography

text: Warren Buffett, like Franklin, explains money in plain words. His yearly letters to his shareholders are read almost like Poor Richard's Almanack.
Both made most of their fortune by letting money grow on itself over a very long time, and both are known for simple, careful habits.
thenNow.trading: Compounding needs time and no big losses. Protect your account first; growth comes from staying in the game.

figures.name: Thomas Edison
figures.tagline: The inventor of the phonograph and a practical light bulb, who built the first invention factory.

lessons.title: Ninety-nine percent work
text: Edison said genius is mostly hard work, not a flash of brilliance.
His lab tested thousands of materials to find a light bulb filament that lasted.
lessons.trading: There is no magic setup. Steady practice, review and patience make a trader.

lessons.title: Every miss is information
text: When a helper felt sorry about thousands of failed tests, Edison said he had lots of results: he now knew thousands of things that didn't work.
A failed test is still a result.
lessons.trading: A losing trade that followed your rules isn't a failure. It's data. Write down what happened and keep going.

lessons.title: Build a system
text: At Menlo Park, Edison built a lab where a team invented things on a schedule. It was the first invention factory.
He turned invention from luck into a process.
lessons.trading: Turn trading into a routine: scan, plan, enter, manage, review. A process you repeat beats waiting for inspiration.

lessons.title: Make it useful
text: Edison aimed his lab at inventions people would actually buy and use: light, sound recording, movies.
Clever doesn't count if nobody can use it.
lessons.trading: Use tools you understand. A simple strategy you follow is worth more than a complicated one you don't.

quotes.text: Genius is one per cent inspiration, ninety-nine per cent perspiration.
quotes.source: Thomas Edison, spoken c. 1903 (as published in Harper's Monthly, September 1932)
quotes.plain: Success comes mostly from hard work, not from being a genius.
quotes.trading: Show up, follow the plan, review. That's the 99%.

quotes.text: Why, man, I have gotten lots of results! I know several thousand things that won't work.
quotes.source: Frank Dyer and T. C. Martin, Edison: His Life and Inventions (1910), as remembered by his associate Walter Mallory
quotes.plain: Each failure taught him something, so none of them was wasted.
quotes.trading: Every losing trade teaches you something, if you write it down.

story: Thomas Edison was born in Ohio in 1847. He had only a few months of school and was taught mostly by his mother.
At 12 he sold newspapers and snacks on trains, and set up a little chemistry lab in a baggage car. He lost most of his hearing as a boy.
He became a telegraph operator, then an inventor. His first patent, a machine to count votes, didn't sell: nobody wanted it. He decided to only invent things people would pay for.
In 1876 he built a laboratory at Menlo Park, New Jersey, with a team that invented on purpose, day after day.
Out came the phonograph (1877), a long-lasting light bulb (1879) and the whole system to power it: in 1882 his Pearl Street station began lighting part of New York. Later came early movie cameras.
He collected 1,093 US patents and died in 1931.

carried.title: Learn from the first flop
carried.text: When his first invention, a vote-counting machine, found no buyers, he decided never again to invent something nobody wanted.
carried.source: Frank Dyer and T. C. Martin, Edison: His Life and Inventions (1910)

carried.title: Work beside the team
carried.text: He worked through the night with his team at Menlo Park and was known to nap on a lab bench or a table before carrying on.
carried.source: Frank Dyer and T. C. Martin, Edison: His Life and Inventions (1910)

carried.title: Calm in a disaster
carried.text: When fire destroyed much of his factory in 1914, his son recalled him calmly watching it and saying they could rebuild. Work started again the next day.
carried.source: As recalled by his son Charles Edison; told in Edmund Morris, Edison (2019)

text: Steve Jobs, like Edison, was less a lone inventor than a builder of teams and products that ordinary people wanted.
Edison sold a whole system (the bulb and the power to run it); Apple sold the device, the software and the store together.
thenNow.trading: Think in systems, not single tricks: your setup, your sizing, your exits and your review all work together.

figures.name: Nikola Tesla
figures.tagline: The inventor of the AC power system that lights the world, who built machines in his head first.

lessons.title: Build it in your head first
text: Tesla said he didn't rush to build. He pictured each machine in his mind, ran it, and fixed it there before touching any metal.
Thinking first saved him months of trial and error.
lessons.trading: Picture the trade before you take it: where you get in, where you're wrong, where you take profit. If you can't see it clearly, don't take it.

lessons.title: A little theory saves a lot of work
text: Tesla once worked for Edison. He felt Edison tried things blindly, when a little math would have saved most of the effort.
Understanding why beats guessing.
lessons.trading: Learn why a setup works (trend, support, volume), not just what it looks like. Then you can spot when it won't work.

lessons.title: Think long term
text: Tesla's AC power won the 'war of the currents' against Edison's DC system and still powers homes today. He kept looking decades ahead.
Big ideas take time to pay off.
lessons.trading: Not every idea is a day trade. The Long-term section of Market is for ideas that need weeks or months to work.

lessons.title: Deep focus
text: Tesla worked long hours alone, deep in one problem at a time.
Big breakthroughs need long stretches without distraction.
lessons.trading: Turn off what distracts you when you study charts. One focused hour beats a whole day half-watching.

quotes.text: My method is different. I do not rush into actual work. When I get an idea I start at once building it up in my imagination.
quotes.source: Nikola Tesla, My Inventions (1919), ch. 1
quotes.plain: He planned everything in his head before doing it for real.
quotes.trading: Plan the whole trade before you click Buy.

quotes.text: The progressive development of man is vitally dependent on invention.
quotes.source: Nikola Tesla, My Inventions (1919), opening line
quotes.plain: People move forward by inventing new things.
quotes.trading: Keep improving your method. What worked last year may need a tweak this year.

quotes.text: If Edison had a needle to find in a haystack, he would proceed at once with the diligence of the bee to examine straw after straw until he found the object of his search.
quotes.source: Nikola Tesla, quoted in The New York Times, 19 October 1931
quotes.plain: Edison worked very hard, but often by brute force instead of thinking first.
quotes.trading: Don't test random ideas on real money. Think first, then test with practice money.

story: Nikola Tesla was born in 1856 in a Serbian family in Smiljan, in today's Croatia. He studied engineering in Austria.
In 1882, walking in a park in Budapest, he suddenly saw how to build a motor run by alternating current (AC), a type of electricity that can travel much further than Edison's DC.
In 1884 he arrived in New York with almost nothing and worked for Edison for a few months, before leaving after a dispute.
After his first company pushed him out, he dug ditches for a living for a while. Then his AC patents were bought by George Westinghouse.
AC won the 'war of the currents', and in 1895 his system powered the great Niagara Falls power station. He went on to work on radio and wireless power.
He was brilliant but bad with money. His big wireless tower project ran out of funding, and he died alone and poor in a New York hotel room in 1943.

carried.title: The idea in the park
carried.text: Walking in Budapest and reciting a poem, he suddenly saw how his AC motor would work, and drew the design in the sand with a stick.
carried.source: Nikola Tesla, My Inventions (1919)

carried.title: Down but not out
carried.text: After his first company pushed him out, he dug ditches for a living. Within about two years, his AC patents were being bought by Westinghouse.
carried.source: W. Bernard Carlson, Tesla: Inventor of the Electrical Age (2013)

carried.title: Running it all in his head
carried.text: He said he could picture a machine so exactly in his mind that he could see which parts would wear out, before building anything.
carried.source: Nikola Tesla, My Inventions (1919)

thenNow.modern: the car company named after him
text: The best-known car company of our time was named after Nikola Tesla when it was founded in 2003, more than 50 years after he died poor.
His ideas paid off hugely, but mostly for others, because he never learned to protect and fund his own work.
thenNow.trading: A great idea isn't enough. In trading, a great entry is wasted without a stop and a plan for taking profit.

pairs.title: Alexander vs Napoleon
pairs.tagline: Napoleon studied Alexander. 2,000 years apart, same playbook.

rounds.a: Struck before enemies were ready, crossing whole countries fast.
rounds.b: Marched faster than any army in Europe by living off the land.

rounds.a: Taught by Aristotle; carried the Iliad on campaign.
rounds.b: Read Alexander's and Caesar's campaigns over and over.

rounds.a: Fought at the front and was wounded many times.
rounds.b: Rose from a young artillery officer and shared his soldiers' hardships on campaign.

rounds.a: Never stopped pushing east, until his own army refused to go on.
rounds.b: Invaded Russia in 1812 and lost most of his army.

pairs.takeaway: Both won with speed and preparation, and both were finally beaten by never knowing when to stop. In trading: plan fast, act fast, and set a point where you stop for the day, even when you are winning.

pairs.title: Edison vs Tesla
pairs.tagline: The tireless tester vs the planner who ran it all in his head.

rounds.a: Try thousands of things until one works.
rounds.b: Picture it, fix it in your head, then build it once.
Invented the AC system, which won and still powers the world.

rounds.a: A great businessman: built companies, sold inventions.
rounds.b: A visionary who was often short of money, and died poor.

rounds.a: Showed that hard work and a system beat waiting for genius.
rounds.b: Showed that deep thinking can skip years of trial and error.

pairs.takeaway: You need both: Tesla's planning before the trade, and Edison's patient testing and record-keeping after it. Plan in your head, test with practice money, write down the results.
